newsitem.title: VATICAN: Vatican envoy slams ethnic violence in Burundi.
newsitem.headline: Vatican envoy slams ethnic violence in Burundi.

text.p: Pope John Paul's envoy to a Mass to mourn Burundi's top Catholic churchman, murdered more than a week ago, slammed ethnic violence and hatred on Tuesday and said its perpetrators would face the wrath of God.

In a sermon prepared for the service in Gitega, where slain Archbishop Joachim Ruhuna headed the diocese, emissary Cardinal Jozef Tomko said ethnic conflict had turned Burundi from the "Switzerland of Africa" into a land of massacre and destruction.
"In the name of God let me say: 'Thou shalt not kill!'," Tomko said in the speech, which was released by the Vatican.
"Woe to those who think to seat their throne on the tombs on the men, women and children of this country," Tomko said.
"The conscience of the world always demands justice for the innocent. And if the wrongdoers escape the justice of men, they will not be able to escape the justice of God."
He appealed to all sides in Burundi, rent by three years of war between ethnic Hutu rebels and the Tutsi-led army, to turn the tiny central African country into a haven of peace.
"To you political leaders, members of different parties, soldiers, armed groups, I say in the name of God: stop massacring the people of Burundi, stop the killing.
"Life comes from God and he will ask all of us to account for the life of our brothers," Tomko said.
Ruhuna and two nuns died when they were ambushed, apparently by rebels. Only the body of one of the nuns has been found.
Four people travelling with them survived the attack north of Gitega, the second largest city in the country.

Tomko said the Pope was saddened by the death of Ruhuna, whose killing he called a grave wound not only to the entire Church but also to the dignity of Burundi, a fiercely Roman Catholic country which he visited in 1990.
"The Holy Father was also serene and confident. Burundi can and must recover," he said.

Fears are widespread that Burundi, ruled since a July 25 coup by Tutsi military strongman Pierre Buyoya, might go the way of its northern neighbour Rwanda, where up to a million people were killed in genocide and three months of civil war in 1994.
The countries have a similar ethnic mix -- overwhelming Hutu majorities with around 15 percent of their populations made up of Tutsis.
